en.sup: Supplied in English. The Greek verb has no object stated.

01.r: Moves from the meal to the reaction of onlookers.

02.r: The Pharisees see who is eating with Jesus.
02.n: An aorist participle, literally 'having seen', with no object; English supplies 'it' or 'this'.

03.r: The Pharisees as a known group.

04.r: Members of the Jewish party known for careful keeping of the law.
04.n: Abbott-Smith traces the name to an Aramaic form, פְּרִישָׁא, and notes that it is usually plural, citing this verse.

05.r: They put their complaint to the disciples.
05.n: An imperfect, 'were saying', which can picture the complaint as ongoing or repeated. The Textus Receptus has the aorist 'they said' instead; see the note on the text.

06.r: The article, in the dative case; with 'his', English needs only 'to'.

07.r: Jesus' followers, not Jesus himself, are the ones addressed.

09.r: With the next word, forms the question 'why'.
09.n: Literally 'on account of what'. English says 'why', so this word has no English of its own.

10.r: Asks the reason, with an edge of objection.

12.r: One article covers both nouns, joining them as a single group.
12.n: Only the ASV and YLT keep it. The single article over 'toll collectors and sinners' treats them as one company, which is how the complaint sees them.

13.r: The toll collectors at the meal.
13.n: This study renders the word 'toll collector' throughout; see the note at Matthew 9:10.

14.r: Joins the two kinds of guest.

16.r: Eating with someone, a sign of fellowship.
16.n: A present tense: he eats with them, now and as his way. That table fellowship was the offence is a reasonable reading of the question, not stated in it.

17.r: With 'your', marks the disciples' own teacher.

18.r: Jesus, as the one the disciples learn from.
18.n: Abbott-Smith notes the word is given as the rendering of Hebrew רַבִּי, rabbi. The older versions' 'Master' is used in the sense of teacher.

tr_note: The Textus Receptus reads εἶπον, the aorist 'they said', where our text has ἔλεγον, the imperfect 'were saying'. The KJV's 'they said' follows the aorist, though most of the later translations also say 'said'.
